newsitem.title: CONGO: Sporadic gunfire disturbs Brazzaville curfew.
newsitem.headline: Sporadic gunfire disturbs Brazzaville curfew.

text.p: Gunshots disturbed a curfew in Congo's capital, Brazzaville, on Thursday night after another day of fighting between supporters of President Pascal Lissouba and his predecessor dashed hopes of a ceasefire.
French army officials said the fighting was less intense than earlier in the week-long conflict, and the shots heard after dark were only sporadic.

But French army spokesman Henry Pelissier said government troops and the Cobra militiamen of former Marxist military leader Denis Sassou Nguesso were still battling for control of the city centre despite their leaders' calls for a truce.
"The Cobras advanced yesterday, although they're still 500 metres (yards) apart. They're not face to face," he said.
Bodies lay unattended in city centre streets. Aid workers and military officials have not been able to reach all areas in order to compile a death toll.
Foreign nationals continued to flee the conflict, which erupted after soldiers surrounded Sassou Nguesso's home as part of a crackdown on private militias before the July 27 presidential election.
Pelissier said France's 1,200 troops had evacuated more than 3,000 foreigners and he estimated that a further 500 Westerners might still need to be brought out.
He played down talk that the French soldiers might intervene directly in the conflict.

"The only mission we have at the moment is to protect and transport foreigners...We don't have a defence accord with Congo and I don't see why at this stage we should put ourselves in the middle as a buffer force," Pelissier said.
Officials in Rome said Italian paratroopers, acting in coordination with the French troops, evacuated 50 Italians and 30 other foreigners from Brazzaville in a military transport plane.
"Despite the risks arising from the tense situation on the ground, the entire Brazzaville operation was carried out without particular difficulty," the Italian Foreign Ministry said.
Medical aid group Medecins Sans Frontieres (Doctors Without Frontiers) said in a statement issued in Paris that it had pulled all its workers out of Congo.
They had been helping 5,000 Rwandan Hutu refugees in a camp at Bilolo, 30 km (20 miles) from Brazzaville.
Automatic gunfire, punctuated by explosions of mortar bombs and rocket-propelled grenades, echoed around the city centre throughout Thursday.
Western military sources said battle lines had remained static in the city centre but the Cobras were advancing in the suburbs towards the zoo along a road to the airport.
"Sadly the ceasefire does not seem to be very much respected," said Congolese army spokesman Colonel Jean-Marie Ompebe.
"We have tried to respect it but if they fire then our men fire back. Sometimes soldiers from both sides just open fire because they are nervous."
